analysis.one_liner: Raises the bar for the government to keep property it seizes without charging the owner with a crime.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan House committee voted 26–0 to advance civil asset forfeiture curbs in June 2023, but the bill never got a vote on the House floor before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it harder for federal agencies to keep cash, cars, homes, and other property seized through civil asset forfeiture — the process by which the government takes property it suspects is tied to a crime, even if the owner is never charged. It would require courts to oversee every forfeiture, raise the government's proof requirement to "clear and convincing evidence," provide a lawyer to people facing loss of their home, and stop agencies from keeping the proceeds, sending them to the Treasury instead. It also adds protections for people whose cash is seized over alleged "structuring" of bank deposits.
analysis.who_benefits: Property owners who are never charged with a crime but have assets seized, especially low-income people who cannot afford a lawyer, people whose homes are targeted, and people whose cash is seized on suspicion of structuring bank deposits. Ordinary taxpayers also benefit in a small way because forfeiture money would go to the general Treasury fund rather than into law enforcement budgets.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every federal forfeiture to go through a court rather than letting agencies forfeit property administratively, with no court order of forfeiture allowed except from a federal district court [S3].

Raises the government's burden of proof from 'preponderance of the evidence' to 'clear and convincing evidence' and requires a substantial connection between the property and an actual offense [S2] [S3].
Requires courts to appoint counsel for an indigent owner whose primary residence faces forfeiture, regardless of whether the owner requests it [S2].

Ends 'equitable sharing' and directs forfeiture proceeds to the Treasury's general fund instead of the DOJ Assets Forfeiture Fund, removing the financial incentive agencies have to seize property [S2] [S3].

Shortens notice deadlines after a seizure from 60 days to 7, cuts the filing window from 90 days after a claim to 30 days after the seizure, and requires a prompt probable cause hearing for seized cash, which must be returned within 14 days absent probable cause [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement agencies, especially the Department of Justice, would lose a revenue stream: the Assets Forfeiture Fund and sharing arrangements that let state and local police receive a cut of federal forfeitures would be curtailed. Prosecutors argue the higher proof standard and abolition of nonjudicial forfeiture would make it harder to strip assets from drug traffickers and to return proceeds to crime victims.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal and local law enforcement budgets

drawbacks.text: Raising the standard to clear and convincing evidence and banning all nonjudicial forfeiture could make it harder and slower to recover money and property from traffickers and to return it to victims of crime [S2] [S3].
Sending proceeds to the general Treasury fund removes a funding source that currently pays for some law enforcement operations, which would have to be replaced through appropriations or lost [S2].
Court-appointed counsel and expedited hearings add costs to the federal court system, and the bill does not provide a dedicated funding source for them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to ordinary people: due-process protections against losing homes, cars, and cash without a criminal conviction, and removal of a profit motive that rewards agencies for seizing property. The costs fall on law enforcement budgets and would make some asset-recovery cases harder, a tradeoff defenders of current law consider too steep. On balance the bill addresses a well-documented grievance — people losing property without being charged — while the costs are mostly administrative and budgetary. The obvious design gap is that it raises court costs without funding them.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it unanimously in June 2023, but House leadership never brought it up for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced in March 2023 by Rep. Tim Walberg with original cosponsors from both parties, including Jamie Raskin, Tom McClintock, Joe Neguse, Kelly Armstrong, and Tony Cárdenas [S1] [S3].
It drew 18 cosponsors, split evenly between 9 House Democrats and 9 House Republicans [S4].
The House Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported, amended, by a 26–0 vote on June 14, 2023 [S5].
No further action followed; the bill was never scheduled for a House floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement agencies keep the current forfeiture system, including the DOJ Assets Forfeiture Fund and equitable sharing payments, and property owners remain subject to the same seizure rules. Members who supported the bill keep a committee vote to point to without ever having to take a recorded floor position that law enforcement groups might oppose.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan at every stage: the six original sponsors split 3–3 between parties, the 18 cosponsors split 9–9, and the Judiciary Committee approved the bill 26–0.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies (DOJ Assets Forfeiture Fund)
industries.note: Agencies would lose the ability to forfeit property without a court order, would face a higher proof standard, and could no longer keep or share the proceeds. Because these agencies currently fund themselves partly through what they seize, their financial interest runs directly against property owners' interests.

industries.industry: State and local police receiving equitable sharing payments
industries.note: The bill eliminates statutory authority for equitable sharing, which lets local police partner with federal agencies and receive a share of forfeiture proceeds. Those departments would lose a revenue channel that bypasses state limits on forfeiture.
The bill creates a right to appointed counsel in home-forfeiture cases and adds expedited hearings, generating work for defense lawyers and the federal courts.
